names.name: The needle now
names.said: What changed in fifty years is not the method

text.what: Single-use needles, gloves and an autoclave are the difference between a hand tradition in 1882 and the same hand tradition today.
text.story:
Shway Yoe's chapter records what the old practice cost: swelling, fever, days of itching, and opium given to boys in doses that occasionally killed them. Milne's Shan boys sat in a circle being told not to scratch. None of that is nostalgia material.

The method did not have to change for that to stop; the supply did. *Inference —* this is the part of a revival that is never a reconstruction, and the practitioners doing it say so themselves.
text.notes: This site carries no medical advice and no aftercare instructions, and nothing here is a recommendation about getting tattooed anywhere.

names.said: Why this site is short of pictures of people

text.what: The free pictures of tattooed bodies are mostly colonial-era photographs of people who did not choose to be photographed, or sideshow portraits made to be sold.
text.story:
A picture can be correctly licensed, on subject, and still be the wrong thing to put in front of a reader. This site's rules on that are simple and were set by its publisher: no blood, no wounds, nothing that turns a person into a specimen, and where a historical photograph is used, it is named for what it is.

The pictures here that show living practice were taken with permission and are credited to the people who gave it.

names.name: What counts as hand-poked
names.said: Tapping is not poking, and both are hands

text.what: The site is called hand poke and half the traditions on it do not poke. Here is the line it draws and why the line is arguable.
text.story:
A poked tattoo is driven by the hand holding the tool. A tapped one is driven by a second stick striking a hafted comb. A stitched one is sewn. A cut one is chiselled or incised and then rubbed with pigment.

All four are hand methods and none of them is a machine, which is why they are all here. But calling them all "hand-poke" flattens the thing each tradition is proudest of, so this site keeps them as four and says which is which on every record.

The hard cases are real. Māori *uhi* work was replaced by needle work in the nineteenth century and the tradition kept its name. Modern professional hand-poke uses a cartridge needle in a stabiliser pen, which is a tool with a handle and a grip and no motor. **A reader who would draw the line somewhere else is looking at the same field on the same records and can re-sort it.**

names.name: Who wrote it down
names.said: An administrator, a doctor, a missionary, an archaeologist

text.what: Most of what is known about the stopped traditions was written by the people whose arrival stopped them.
text.story:
Shway Yoe was Sir James George Scott, who wrote as a Burman and spent his career extending British rule over the Shan States. Leopold Glück was a doctor in occupied Bosnia. Ćiro Truhelka was an archaeologist in the same administration. Hose and McDougall were a colonial officer and a psychologist. The Gazetteer of Upper Burma is a government publication, and in the middle of a paragraph about Chin women's faces it stops to insult them.

This site uses all of it, because there is nothing else, and it names the writer every time. **The detail is usually reliable and the frame usually is not** — a measurement of a tool, a rate of work, a fee, an age, a sequence, these are the things an observer can get right. Why people did it, what they believed, what it meant: on those, the source is guessing about people it does not respect.

The Lanna volume in the corpus is the counter-case on this site, and that is why it is quoted at length: same region, same custom, written from inside it.

names.name: Whose designs
names.said: Closed motifs, earned marks, and a queue of visitors

text.what: Several traditions on this site hold that certain designs may not be worn by people who have not earned them. That rule is theirs to state and not this site's to adjudicate.
text.story:
Cordilleran elders hold that copying an old warrior's chest design marks a person as a killer and brings bad luck, blindness or an early death — and men who fought in the 1960s and 70s declined the marks on that advice. Kalinga inheritance rules held that tattooing could only pass down a bloodline. Sak yant carries rules the bearer keeps afterwards. *Moko kauae* is worn by Māori women.

What this site does: state the rule where a tradition states it, name who states it, and print no design as available. What this site does not do: decide who may wear what, or rank the arguments.
